title: Elimination of Early and Forced Marriage

headings.title: Introduction to Early and Forced Marriage
headings.content: Early and forced marriage (EFM) remains a critical public health and human rights issue globally, with a disproportionate burden borne by young girls in low- and middle-income countries, including Nigeria. Defined as any formal marriage or informal union where one or both parties are under the age of 18, early marriage deprives children of their fundamental rights to education, health, and personal development. For nursing and midwifery students in Nigeria, understanding EFM is essential because it intersects directly with maternal and child health. Young brides are frequently pressured into premature sexual activity and childbearing before their bodies are biologically mature, leading to catastrophic obstetric complications such as obstetric fistula, severe postpartum hemorrhage, and high rates of maternal and neonatal mortality. Furthermore, early marriage perpetuates cycles of poverty, disempowers women, and limits national development. Healthcare professionals must recognize that EFM is not merely a private family matter, but a profound violation of human rights that requires urgent multi-sectoral intervention. By examining the structural roots and health impacts of this practice, nurses can better advocate for vulnerable populations, educate communities, and implement targeted care strategies to protect adolescent girls and promote gender equality across Nigerian healthcare settings.

headings.title: Underlying Socio-Cultural and Economic Drivers
headings.content: The persistence of early and forced marriage in Nigeria is deeply rooted in a complex interplay of socio-cultural norms, religious misinterpretations, and severe economic hardship. In many traditional communities, patriarchal structures view young girls as economic burdens or financial assets to be exchanged for bride price, dowries, or to settle familial debts. Poverty acts as a powerful catalyst; families struggling for daily survival may marry off their daughters early to reduce household expenses or secure financial relief. Additionally, deeply entrenched cultural beliefs regarding female sexuality, honor, and chastity drive families to marry off girls prematurely to prevent premarital pregnancies that could allegedly bring shame to the household. Educational deprivation further compounds the issue, as out-of-school girls are significantly more vulnerable to early unions due to a lack of economic alternatives and empowerment. Furthermore, harmful traditional practices and weak enforcement of protective laws sustain these cultural norms, making them socially acceptable in certain regions. Nurses and midwives must comprehend these underlying socioeconomic and cultural drivers to design culturally sensitive educational programs and engage community and religious leaders effectively in dismantling the justifications used to uphold early and forced marriage.

headings.title: Physical and Psychological Health Consequences
headings.content: The physical and psychological health consequences of early and forced marriage on young girls are profound, lifelong, and often devastating. Physically, adolescent bodies are unprepared for pregnancy and childbirth; the pelvis is underdeveloped, leading to prolonged and obstructed labor, high rates of cesarean sections, obstetric fistula, and severe maternal morbidity or mortality. Infants born to young mothers also face higher risks of premature birth, low birth weight, and neonatal death. Sexually transmitted infections, including HIV, are more prevalent among married adolescents due to power imbalances that prevent them from negotiating safe sex or refusing unwanted sexual advances from older partners. Psychologically, the trauma of forced sexual initiation, social isolation, and the sudden cessation of childhood leads to high rates of anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and suicidal ideation. These girls are abruptly cut off from their peers, schools, and support systems, leaving them feeling trapped and powerless. For nursing and midwifery students, recognizing these interconnected health crises is vital for delivering holistic care that addresses not only the physical injuries and obstetric emergencies of young brides, but also their mental health and emotional healing needs.

headings.title: Human Rights and Legal Frameworks in Nigeria
headings.content: Addressing early and forced marriage in Nigeria requires a thorough understanding of the national and international human rights and legal frameworks designed to protect children. Internationally, conventions such as the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), alongside the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, explicitly prohibit marriage before the age of 18 and guarantee the right to education and health. Nationally, the Child Rights Act (CRA) was enacted in 2003 to domesticate international standards, setting the legal age of marriage at 18 years. However, the implementation of the CRA remains decentralized and inconsistent across Nigeria's 36 states, with some northern states failing to domesticate or fully enforce the act due to conflicting customary and Sharia legal provisions. Furthermore, the Nigerian Constitution contains ambiguities regarding age of majority and marital capacity, creating legal loopholes that perpetrators exploit. Nurses and midwives must be knowledgeable about these legal frameworks to recognize statutory violations, understand mandatory reporting obligations where applicable, and collaborate with social welfare and legal authorities to advocate effectively for the enforcement of child protection laws.

headings.title: The Role of Nurses and Midwives in Prevention and Identification
headings.content: Nurses and midwives occupy a frontline position in the healthcare system, making them uniquely situated to identify, prevent, and respond to early and forced marriage. In clinical settings such as antenatal clinics, immunization units, and emergency departments, nurses must remain vigilant for red flags, such as young pregnant girls accompanied by much older spouses, signs of physical abuse, untreated sexually transmitted infections, or sudden school dropouts. Midwives providing intrapartum care must be sensitive to the unique physical needs of underage mothers, offering compassionate, non-judgmental care while recognizing the signs of forced unions. Prevention efforts also involve health education; nurses can use routine patient interactions to educate adolescents and parents about the health risks of early childbearing and the importance of keeping girls in school. Moreover, nurses must establish a safe, confidential environment that encourages young girls to disclose coercion or abuse. When EFM is identified, nurses have a professional and ethical duty to initiate multidisciplinary referrals, collaborating with social workers, legal aid organizations, and child protection agencies to ensure the safety and rehabilitation of the affected minor.

headings.title: Community-Based Interventions and Advocacy Strategies
headings.content: Combating early and forced marriage effectively requires robust community-based interventions and strategic advocacy that target the root causes of the practice at the grassroots level. Nurses and healthcare educators cannot work in isolation; they must partner with traditional rulers, religious leaders, youth groups, and local women's associations who hold significant influence over community norms and behaviors. Community dialogues and educational workshops are powerful tools to challenge harmful patriarchal beliefs, promote the value of girl-child education, and reframe cultural practices in ways that respect human rights. Advocacy strategies should also involve empowering young girls through life-skills training, mentorship programs, and economic support initiatives that demonstrate their value beyond marriage. Furthermore, establishing community watch committees or school-based protection clubs can help identify at-risk girls before marriages are finalized. By working collaboratively within communities, nurses help foster local ownership of child protection initiatives, ensuring sustainable behavioral change and creating an environment where early and forced marriage is actively rejected by community members themselves.

headings.title: Support, Rehabilitation, and Care for Survivors
headings.content: Providing comprehensive support, rehabilitation, and care for survivors of early and forced marriage is essential for their successful reintegration into society and long-term well-being. Survivors often present with complex medical needs, requiring specialized obstetric care, fistula repair surgeries, nutritional rehabilitation, and ongoing management of chronic reproductive tract infections. Beyond physical care, mental health support is paramount; professional psychological counseling, trauma-informed therapy, and support groups help survivors process their experiences, rebuild self-esteem, and overcome anxiety and depression. Educational and economic rehabilitation is equally critical to break the cycle of dependency and poverty. Safe shelters, vocational training programs, and scholarships enable survivors to resume their education or acquire marketable skills, fostering financial independence and autonomy. Nurses and midwives play an integral role in this multidisciplinary rehabilitation team by providing empathetic, trauma-informed care, coordinating comprehensive care plans, and advocating for holistic social support services that empower survivors to reclaim their futures with dignity.
